query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In pre-exposure Q235 steel, the spontaneous formation of a nanometric passive oxide film governs the early stages of corrosion: its integrity and defect density determine whether localized pit nucleation occurs. At elevated temperatures, accelerated oxide film formation produces a denser, more protective layer that suppresses pit initiation relative to room-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pristine, unmodified (pre-exposure) state
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to a controlled corrosive medium (saline/acidic solution) in a temperature-controlled electrochemical cell equipped with real-time surface imaging (e.g., in situ scanning probe microscopy or synchrotron X-ray methods) at room temperature (~25 °C) and selected elevated temperatures (e.g., 50–100 °C)
generation.conditions: Harsh corrosive environments created by saline or acidic solutions under identical mechanical and thermal loads, with one set of samples maintained at room temperature and another set subjected to elevated temperatures
generation.structural_mediator: The spontaneous passive oxide film that forms on the steel surface, whose composition, thickness, and defect density modulate local electrochemical conditions
generation.mechanism: The hypothesis posits that corrosion onset is driven by the localized breakdown or protection of the passive oxide film: at room temperature, the film may develop defects that facilitate pit nucleation through localized pH and potential fluctuations, while at elevated temperatures, the accelerated growth kinetics yield a denser, defect-reduced film that suppresses pit initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ observations are expected to show an earlier onset of localized pitting and higher corrosion current densities at room temperature, whereas at elevated temperatures, a more uniform and stable oxide film will be evident, with delayed (or reduced) pit nucleation and lower corrosion current densities compared to untreated references.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel samples maintained in a non-corrosive (inert) environment to monitor the natural oxide formation in the absence of aggressive chemical or temperature stimuli
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable solely to Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state under the specified corrosive media and thermal conditions. Variations in surface contaminants, alloying elements, or additional mechanical stresses could alter the observed effects.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed experiment is designed to deconvolute the role of the passive film, the relative contributions of other electrochemical factors (such as local pH shifts and microstructural heterogeneities) remain uncertain and may require further detailed characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ corrosion experiment using a temperature-controlled electrochemical cell with real-time surface imaging on Q235 steel samples. Prepare two groups: one maintained at room temperature and the other at a selected elevated temperature in an identical saline (or acidic) environment. Monitor and record the initiation and progression of pit nucleation events, the evolution of the oxide film, and corrosion current densities for both groups. A third group maintained in an inert, non-corrosive environment shall serve as a control for natural oxide formation.
measurements: Time-resolved imaging of the steel surface to detect pit nucleation and oxide layer evolution
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess the integrity and resistance of the passive oxide film
Tafel analysis to quantify corrosion current densities
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS) to characterize the composition and defect density of the oxide film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature condition does not result in a demonstrably denser and more protective oxide film—with no significant difference in pit nucleation timing, corrosion current density, or film integrity compared to the room-temperature condition—the hypothesis that temperature-induced enhanced oxide film formation suppresses early-stage corrosion would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additionally, DFT was used to study the oxidation thermodynamics of Nb–Ti binary alloys and to calculate the oxide composition and structural changes during the oxidation process, offering an effective method for analysing oxidation processes in HEAs []. To summarize, the mechanisms of high-temperature oxidation in CrMnFeCoNi system reported in references [,,,] were mainly based upon surface analysis of the reaction products retained after tests, which is insufficient because great emphasis has been placed on post-mortem analyses of reaction products analysed at ambient temperature, or else assumptions made via the analysis of the temperature dependence of phases at different temperatures. Clearly, this introduces a degree of uncertainty, since one cannot be completely sure of the underlying physical mechanisms which are imperative on the critical scales: that of the activity of elements, transformation temperatures, and vapour pressure at the same time. Time–temperature-resolved in situ XRD observations would be invaluable in circumventing this ambiguity and in elucidating the chemical processes giving rise to the oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi alloy.

In this work, we present an equiatomic CoNiV MEA, which maintains its good mechanical performance under the impact of hydrogen, i.e., the material under investigation shows no obvious hydrogen embrittlement at a temperature of 300 K and a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, and it has good corrosion resistance when exposed to acidic environments. This property synergy, balancing strength, ductility, corrosion, and hydrogen embrittlement, is realized by four main effects: The alloy’s solid solution hardened single face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) phase structure, devoid of any precipitations, provides both, (1) low hydrogen diffusivity and (2) absence of local electrochemical potential gradients. (3) The solute hydrogen in the bulk alloy matrix leads to the formation of deformation twins which impede crack propagation during slow strain rate tensile testing,. (4) The formation of an oxide barrier film with low concentrations of point defects, i.e., metal and oxygen vacancies and metal interstitials, and low content of Co- and Ni-containing hydroxides on the alloy surface in sulfuric acid solution acts as an efficient barrier against oxygen transport, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance. decision.trend: From 2019 onward, several studies have focused on uncovering how multi-principal element alloys or advanced alloy coatings resist corrosive attack—often through targeted microstructural refinements and protective surface layers. In 2019 (PMC6908586), researchers investigated corrosion in molten salt environments at high temperatures, highlighting how element dissolution and oxide formation affect corrosion performance. By 2020 (PMC7299985), emphasis shifted toward multi-component alloys that mitigate hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion via dense oxide films and defect-tolerant microstructures. In 2021 (PMC8305802), depositing corrosion-resistant high-entropy coatings onto a steel substrate demonstrated improved barrier qualities, linking local composition-structure features to environmental durability. Most recently (PMC10744552, 2023), advanced thermomechanical treatments were explored for enhancing both mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, underscoring how phase transformations and oxide film integrity govern corrosion onset. Despite progress, isolating the fundamental, temperature- and environment-dependent mechanisms that trigger or prevent steel corrosion remains a key open question, especially for conventional grades such as Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state.
decision.unsolved: Although various pathways for corrosion mitigation have been proposed—ranging from microstructural engineering to protective coatings—clear, experimentally validated cause–effect mechanisms at the earliest stages of corrosion in standard structural steels remain elusive. In particular, it is still difficult to distinguish whether initial corrosion stems from localized electrochemical phenomena, breakdown of near-surface films, or changes in steel microstructure under different temperature and chemical conditions. A definitive study that separates these effects for Q235 steel will enable prediction and control of corrosion onset or suppression in harsh environments.
decision.lever: Use temperature-controlled electrochemical cell with real-time surface imaging (e.g., scanning probe or synchrotron X-ray methods) to track early pit nucleation and oxide evolution on Q235 steel at 25 °C and elevated temperatures in a corrosive medium (e.g., saline or acidic environment). Compare results to non-exposed references under identical mechanical and thermal loads to pinpoint the relative roles of protective film breakdown, local pH changes, and microstructure transformations in initiating or preventing corrosion.
decision.why: Recent research emphasizes complex metallurgical or surface-based solutions but lacks clarity on simplified, direct tests that deconvolute the mechanistic triggers of corrosion under different temperature and chemical exposures. An in situ characterization design would allow real-time observation of incipient corrosion events, enabling a decisive test of whether film breakdown, local environment shifts, or phase/microstructure changes dominate early-stage degradation in Q235 steel.
